name: FM radio
description: Wideband FM broadcast with RDS station text.
explainer: The wide humps across the display are FM stations, each about 200 kHz across. The channel is tuned to one of them; RDS decodes the station name and radio text from a subcarrier you cannot hear. Drag the channel marker or edit its offset to move between stations.

name: Airband
description: AM aircraft voice: tower, approach and ground.
explainer: Civil aviation voice is AM between 118 and 137 MHz, 25 kHz apart. Transmissions are short and sporadic: leave the squelch on and wait. The 2.4 MHz window covers roughly 117–119.3 MHz, so tower, ground and approach are usually all reachable by moving the channel offset alone. 121.5 MHz is the emergency frequency and is normally silent.

name: Aircraft (ADS-B)
description: 1090 MHz aircraft positions on the map.
explainer: Aircraft broadcast their identity, altitude, speed and position on 1090 MHz. Reception is line-of-sight, so range depends on antenna height far more than on gain.

name: Aircraft data (ACARS)
description: Airline datalink text on the VHF ACARS channels.
explainer: ACARS carries short text between aircraft and their airline: position reports, weather, link tests, gate changes and maintenance messages. The allocation is regional, so five channels are decoded at once: 131.550 MHz is the worldwide primary, 131.725 MHz serves Europe and 131.425 MHz the Asia-Pacific region. Traffic is bursty: near a busy airport expect a message every few seconds, elsewhere a handful per hour.

name: Ships (AIS)
description: Marine AIS positions on the map.
explainer: Ships broadcast position and identity on two VHF channels, 161.975 and 162.025 MHz. Both channels are decoded at once. Coverage is line-of-sight over water, which is usually far better than over land.

name: APRS
description: Amateur position and message packets (144.800 MHz).
explainer: APRS is AX.25 packet radio at 1200 baud AFSK. Each burst is a short chirp; stations report position, weather or messages. 144.800 MHz is the European calling frequency: North America uses 144.390 MHz.

name: Pagers
description: POCSAG, FLEX and ERMES pager messages.
explainer: Pager traffic still carries hospital, industrial and emergency dispatch messages. The three decoders cover POCSAG at every standard baud rate, all four FLEX modes and European ERMES. Frequencies are regional; check your national allocation before tuning.

name: Railroad EOT
description: End-of-Train brake pressure, motion and marker light.
explainer: North American freight trains carry an End-of-Train unit that reports rear brake pipe pressure, motion and battery on 457.9375 MHz. The locomotive answers and sends emergency commands on 452.9375 MHz; retune the channel there to log them.

name: NOAA Weather Radio
description: Forecast voice plus the SAME alert headers that drive it.
explainer: The seven NWR channels between 162.400 and 162.550 MHz carry continuous forecast voice. An alert is announced by a SAME header burst sent three times before the voice and closed by an end-of-message burst after it. The speaker plays the voice; the SAME node logs the event code, the counties it covers and how long it stays valid. Retune both channels to whichever of the seven your transmitter uses.

name: 406 MHz beacons
description: EPIRB, ELT and PLB identity and position.
explainer: Distress beacons send a half-second burst every 50 seconds between 406.0 and 406.1 MHz. The channel covers 406.024 to 406.044 MHz, where most beacons sit. Self-test bursts are marked as such.

name: Drone Remote ID
description: Drone ID, position and pilot over Bluetooth.
explainer: Drones broadcast their serial number, position and pilot location under ASTM F3411 and EN 4709-002. Bluetooth 4 adverts arrive on channel 38; Bluetooth 5 long range puts its data on the channels around it.

name: Drone Remote ID · Wi-Fi
description: Drone ID, position and pilot from Wi-Fi beacons.
explainer: DJI and many other drones send Remote ID in Wi-Fi beacons, usually on channel 6. Retune to channel 1, 11 or 149 if nothing shows.

name: BLE devices
description: Bluetooth LE devices, beacons and trackers.
explainer: Phones, tags and sensors advertise on channel 38. A 20 MS/s window also hears long range adverts on the data channels around it.

name: 433 MHz sensors
description: Weather stations, thermometers, remotes and door sensors.
explainer: Decodes OOK and FSK sensors the way rtl_433 does. Tick unknown to also log repeated codes no decoder knows.

name: 868 MHz meters
description: Water, heat and energy meters.
explainer: Reads wireless M-Bus modes T and C. Add a meter's key to open encrypted readings.

name: 2.4 GHz survey
description: Who uses 2.4 GHz: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Zigbee, ovens.
explainer: Sorts every burst by width, length and channel grid, from energy alone. One report per second.

name: Wi-Fi occupancy
description: How busy each Wi-Fi channel is.
explainer: Busy time from energy alone, once a second. A 20 MS/s radio sees one channel; 80 MS/s sees all of 2.4 GHz.

name: Noise figure
description: Receiver noise figure with a switched noise source.
explainer: Feed a calibrated noise source into the antenna port, set its ENR and switch it on and off. Each switch settles a new Y-factor reading.

name: PER tester
description: Packet and bit error rate of PER test frames.
explainer: Counts numbered 2-FSK test frames and compares each payload with its known PRBS9 pattern. The signal generator sends them as PER test frames.

name: SID monitor
description: Solar flares in VLF transmitter levels.
explainer: Flares lift or dip daytime VLF signals for minutes to hours. Needs a radio that reaches 16 to 46 kHz and a long wire or loop.

name: Radio clock
description: DCF77 civil time and minute-code inspection.
explainer: DCF77 lowers its 77.5 kHz carrier once per second. The pulse width carries the next minute's time and date, with separate parity checks for minute, hour and calendar fields. Select WWVB, MSF or JJY in the channel settings and retune to the service used in your region.

name: NAVTEX
description: Coastal navigation warnings on 490 and 518 kHz.
explainer: NAVTEX broadcasts navigational and meteorological warnings to ships as 100 baud FSK teleprinter text. 518 kHz carries the international English service, 490 kHz the national-language one, and both are decoded here. Stations transmit on a schedule a few times a day, so leave it running; reception is far better after dark.

name: GNSS lab
description: Inspect GPS L1 C/A acquisition and NAV subframes.
explainer: This educational receiver searches one GPS PRN at a time so the code phase, Doppler and correlation strength stay visible. After acquisition it checks the 50 bit/s navigation-word parity and reports subframe ID, time of week and the truncated GPS week from subframe 1. It is not a navigation-grade position solution.

name: Ham 2 m
description: The 2 metre amateur band, FM repeater output segment.
explainer: 145.600–145.800 MHz carries FM repeater outputs, 12.5 kHz apart. Point the scanner at this range to find the active ones: a repeater is silent between overs, so a sweep finds far more than sitting on one channel.

name: Marine VHF
description: Marine voice on channel 16 and DSC alerts on channel 70.
explainer: Channel 16 (156.800 MHz) is the international distress and calling channel and is monitored everywhere; working traffic moves off it. Marine VHF is narrowband FM, 25 kHz apart. Channel 70 (156.525 MHz) carries DSC distress and calling alerts.

name: PMR446 walkie-talkies
description: The eight classic licence-free FM channels at 446 MHz.
explainer: PMR446 handsets are sold without a licence across Europe, so this is the band with the most everyday traffic: markets, building sites, ski slopes and events. Channels 1–8 sit 12.5 kHz apart from 446.00625 MHz and all eight are open at once, each with automatic squelch so only a real transmission reaches the speaker. The readout shows the CTCSS or DCS code a handset sends, which is what its 'privacy code' setting really is. Channels 9–16 continue to 446.19375 MHz and are visible on the scope.

name: Digital voice (70 cm)
description: DMR, D-STAR, System Fusion and M17 decoded side by side.
explainer: Amateur repeaters carry four incompatible digital voice systems that all look alike on a waterfall. Running one decoder per system on the same frequency answers which is in use: whichever locks is the mode, and the log names the talkgroup, callsign or reflector it carries while the speaker plays the decoded voice. Retune the receiver to a repeater output near you: 439 MHz is only the middle of the segment.

name: TETRA cell
description: Cell identity, calls and short messages of a TETRA carrier.
explainer: Tune to a TETRA downlink. The log names the network, location area and carrier, then each call setup, talker and SDS. Voice is not decoded, and air-encrypted cells only show their identity. 392.5 MHz is only an example.

name: DAB ensemble check
description: Confirm a DAB block is on air and measure its lock.
explainer: A DAB ensemble is one 1.536 MHz wide OFDM block carrying a bundle of stations. This template locks to the block's transmission frame and reports lock, signal-to-noise and frequency error, which is what an antenna or filter change has to improve before anything else matters. It does not play DAB audio. 178.352 MHz is block 5C; the channel settings list the other blocks.

name: HF digital (20 m)
description: FT8, FT4 and WSPR decoded together on 20 metres.
explainer: These three modes trade speed for sensitivity and decode signals well below the noise floor, which is why 20 m stays busy even when the band sounds empty. FT8 (14.074 MHz) and FT4 (14.080 MHz) are contacts on a 15 and 7.5 second clock; WSPR (14.0956 MHz) is beacons on a two-minute one. Decoding depends on the computer clock being right: an error over about a second costs you every FT8 slot.

name: HF keyboard modes (20 m)
description: CW, RTTY and PSK31 read as text, with the audio to match.
explainer: The oldest live modes on the band are still hand-tuned: each decoder is only a few hundred hertz wide, so drag its marker onto a trace on the scope until the text comes out clean. 14.100 MHz carries the international beacon project, whose eighteen stations transmit their callsign in Morse in turn, so it is the one frequency here that is busy on a schedule. The SSB channel demodulates the same segment so you hear what the decoders are reading.

name: SSTV pictures (20 m)
description: Slow-scan television on 14.230 MHz, picture and sound.
explainer: SSTV sends a still picture as audio, one line at a time, in one to two minutes. The mode is announced by a VIS header at the start of a transmission and detected for you, so a picture starts building as soon as one is received. 14.230 MHz is the worldwide calling frequency; the SSB channel plays the warble the decoder is turning into the image.

name: HF data modems
description: Names STANAG, MIL-STD-188-110 and 2G ALE signals.
explainer: Put the channel on the USB dial of a data signal. The identifier names the modem, its carrier and, for MIL-STD-188-110A, the rate from its preamble.

name: Weather satellites (137.9 MHz)
description: Meteor-M LRPT pictures during a pass.
explainer: Meteor-M N2-4 sends a digital picture on 137.900 MHz while it passes overhead, OQPSK at 72k. It is the last 137 MHz weather satellite: the NOAA APT ones left the air in August 2025. Use the Satellite node for Doppler.

name: Weather fax (HF)
description: DWD weather charts from Pinneberg on 7.880 MHz.
explainer: Radiofax sends weather charts line by line. Start and stop tones begin and end a chart; the start tone picks the IOC for you. Channels sit on the USB carrier, 1.9 kHz below the published frequency.

name: Radiosondes (403 MHz)
description: Weather balloon position and readings, RS41, DFM, M10, M20, iMet.
explainer: Weather services launch radiosondes once or twice a day. Each sends its position, temperature, humidity and pressure every second. Set the channel to your nearest launch site's frequency.

name: Aircraft data (VDL2)
description: VHF Data Link Mode 2 messages from aircraft.
explainer: VDL2 replaces ACARS on busy routes, at 31.5 kbit/s. 136.975 MHz is the common channel; Europe adds 136.725, 136.775 and 136.875 MHz.

name: Aircraft data (HFDL)
description: HF datalink from aircraft over oceans.
explainer: Aircraft far from land send position reports and messages on HF. Ground stations change frequency with the time of day; these are four around 10 MHz.

name: Aircraft (UAT 978)
description: US aircraft positions and FIS-B weather on 978 MHz.
explainer: General aviation in the US sends positions on 978 MHz instead of 1090 MHz. Ground stations add weather and traffic.

name: VOR and ILS
description: Bearing to a VOR and deviation from an ILS localizer.
explainer: Set each channel to a beacon near you: VORs sit on even tenths from 108 MHz, localizers on odd tenths below 112 MHz.

name: Inmarsat Aero
description: Aircraft datalink relayed by Inmarsat.
explainer: Aircraft messages relayed by geostationary satellites near 1545 MHz. Point a patch antenna at the satellite and retune to its channel.

name: Inmarsat C (EGC)
description: Maritime safety and text messages by satellite.
explainer: EGC carries navigational warnings and weather for ships. 1537.70 MHz is the EMEA satellite; other regions use other channels.

name: Iridium bursts
description: Ring alerts and bursts from Iridium satellites.
explainer: Iridium satellites pass every few minutes. The simplex channels at 1626 MHz carry ring alerts with the satellite position.

name: GOES HRIT
description: GOES-R pictures and bulletins at 1694.1 MHz.
explainer: GOES-East and GOES-West are geostationary: point a dish once and receive full disk pictures all day.

name: GK-2A LRIT
description: GK-2A pictures and bulletins at 1692.14 MHz.
explainer: GK-2A covers Asia and the Pacific from 128.2° east. A small dish is enough.

name: HRPT (L band)
description: Full resolution pictures from polar weather satellites.
explainer: Meteor-M, NOAA and MetOp send HRPT near 1700 MHz during a pass. A tracked dish or helix is needed; use the Satellite node for Doppler.

name: NOAA APT
description: Pictures from NOAA APT pass recordings.
explainer: NOAA 15, 18 and 19 left the air in 2025. Play an old pass recording on the Device.

name: Horus balloons
description: Horus Binary telemetry from high-altitude balloons.
explainer: Amateur balloons send position and sensors on 434 MHz, often near 434.200 MHz.

name: Wenet pictures
description: Live pictures from amateur balloons.
explainer: Wenet sends JPEG pictures at 115 kbit/s, usually on 443.500 MHz.

name: LoRa and Meshtastic (868 MHz)
description: LoRaWAN and Meshtastic packets in the EU band.
explainer: 868.1 MHz is a LoRaWAN uplink channel; 869.525 MHz is the Meshtastic EU default.

name: DECT phones
description: DECT cordless phone carriers and calls.
explainer: DECT uses ten carriers from 1881.792 to 1897.344 MHz. Retune to the one your scope shows busy.

name: GSM cell
description: Cell identity and broadcast of a GSM carrier.
explainer: Tune to a cell's broadcast carrier. 935.2 MHz is ARFCN 1 of GSM 900.

name: Signal identifier
description: Guesses what an unknown signal is.
explainer: Put the channel on a signal you do not know; the readout names the most likely mode.

name: HD Radio
description: NRSC-5 station information and digital audio.
explainer: HD Radio adds digital sidebands to US FM stations. Retune to a station near you.

name: DRM shortwave
description: Digital Radio Mondiale broadcasts.
explainer: Few stations broadcast DRM. Look up a schedule and retune to one.

name: DVB-T
description: A DVB-T or T2 multiplex.
explainer: 506 MHz is UHF channel 25. Retune to a multiplex near you.

name: Analog ATV (23 cm)
description: Amateur analog TV picture and sound.
explainer: Amateur ATV repeaters often output on 23 cm. Retune to one near you.

name: Digital ATV (70 cm)
description: DVB-S and S2 amateur TV.
explainer: Digital amateur TV on 437 MHz. Retune to a repeater or station near you.

name: Professional digital voice
description: P25, NXDN and Tetrapol side by side.
explainer: One decoder per system on the same frequency: whichever locks is the mode. Retune to a channel near you.

name: Trunk control channels
description: MPT 1327, EDACS and LTR side by side.
explainer: One decoder per system on the same frequency: whichever locks names the system. Retune to a control channel near you.

name: dPMR446
description: Licence-free digital walkie-talkies at 446 MHz.
explainer: dPMR446 has 16 channels 6.25 kHz apart from 446.103125 MHz. This is channel 1.

name: FM signalling
description: DTMF, Selcall, MDC-1200 and FleetSync on one FM channel.
explainer: Business and public service radios send IDs and digits before a call. Retune to a channel near you.

name: Benshi chat
description: Chat, positions and calls from Benshi handhelds.
explainer: Benshi handhelds send text and positions on any channel. 145.500 MHz is the 2 m calling channel.

name: FreeDV (20 m)
description: HF digital voice on 14.236 MHz.
explainer: FreeDV 1600 fits voice into 1.25 kHz. 14.236 MHz is the 20 m activity frequency.

name: CW skimmer (20 m)
description: Every Morse signal in the CW segment at once.
explainer: Each signal is decoded and logged with its call. Spots appear as stations call CQ.

name: JT65, JT9 and JS8 (20 m)
description: Older weak signal modes and JS8Call chat.
explainer: JT65 on 14.076 MHz, JT9 and JS8 on 14.078 MHz. Decoding needs an accurate clock.

name: 6 m scatter
description: MSK144 meteor pings and Q65 on 6 metres.
explainer: Meteor trails reflect 6 m for a fraction of a second. MSK144 catches those pings on 50.260 MHz; Q65 handles scatter and EME on 50.275 MHz.

name: FST4 and FST4W (630 m)
description: LF and MF weak signal contacts and beacons.
explainer: FST4W beacons and FST4 contacts share the 630 m dial on 474.2 kHz.
